input.summary: The claim asserts 99.99% optical-link terminal availability over LEO passes. No hardware, orbital trace, atmospheric model, or availability definition has been supplied. Built-in transport runners (netem/iperf) cannot substitute for optical-terminal or orbital availability measurement. Before a feasible pilot can be proposed, several foundational decisions must be resolved.
clarification_questions: What is the precise operational definition of 'availability' for this claim — e.g., fraction of scheduled LEO pass time during which the optical link meets a specified BER/SNR threshold, fraction of passes with at least one successful acquisition, or some other metric — and over what observation window (number of passes, calendar duration) is 99.99% asserted?

What evidence source or model is intended to support the pilot — e.g., a specific versioned atmospheric/orbital simulation tool with a supplied input trace, archived terminal telemetry from a prior campaign, or a new empirical measurement campaign — and can you supply the identity (name, version, hash) of that source or dataset?

If a simulation path is intended, which versioned simulation package (e.g., a specific link-budget or orbital-pass availability model) would be used, and can you supply its version identifier and a description of the input parameters (orbital altitude, terminal aperture, atmospheric model, pointing-loss budget) so that a custom-package protocol can be scoped?
